title: Levamisole-induced vasculitis: A characteristic cutaneous vasculitis associated with levamisole-adulterated cocaine

claims.statement: As described in two narrative reviews (Buchanan & Lavonas, 2012; Roberts & Chévez-Barrios, 2015; no systematic search or appraisal; all figures second-hand), levamisole, a veterinary medicine used mainly against worms in cattle, sheep and pigs and formerly used in people for autoimmune conditions and some cancers, was found in much of the cocaine sold in the United States around 2010: the US Drug Enforcement Administration first detected it in seized cocaine in 2003 and, by a figure the review does not source, in 73.2% of the cocaine it analysed in January 2010; in seizures in Luxembourg it was the commonest adulterant, at 1.5% to 4.1% of the sample; studies published in 2011 found it in 78% (Denver) and 88% (San Francisco) of urine samples from hospital patients that screened positive for cocaine metabolites; and the later review states that about 70% of US cocaine contains it. Case reports and small series from 2009 onward, first from Alberta, British Columbia, New Mexico, Washington, Arizona and Colorado, describe two conditions in people who had smoked, injected or snorted cocaine. One is agranulocytosis, an almost complete loss of the neutrophil white blood cells that fight infection, most often after smoking: neutrophil counts recovered within about 2 to 3 days of hospital treatment with GCSF in most case reports and within about 5 to 10 days after exposure ended without it, and about half of the patients in one series had more than one episode when they used cocaine again. The other is a skin vasculopathy: painful purple patches in a net-like or star-shaped pattern, sometimes with blisters and dead skin, typically on the ears, cheeks, nose and limbs, with autoantibodies (such as ANCA), clotted small vessels and/or inflamed vessel walls on biopsy, and neutropenia in about half of cases; women made up most of the reported cases although more men use cocaine. The lesions usually resolved within a few weeks after cocaine use stopped, though some patients needed removal of dead tissue, skin grafts or amputation; no treatment has been tested in a controlled study. The cases were attributed to levamisole mainly from their pattern, from the person's cocaine use (by history or a urine test for a cocaine metabolite) and from the same effects seen when levamisole was used as a medicine: the first in-depth case report with laboratory confirmation of levamisole appeared in early 2010; levamisole leaves the blood within about a day (plasma half-life about 5.6 hours, a figure the earlier review does not source) and stays detectable in urine for about 2 to 3 days; and the later review states that testing for it is not needed for diagnosis because it is so common in cocaine, so cases were often attributed without measuring it, and since most people who use cocaine would test positive, a positive test shows exposure rather than cause. A brain disorder (leukoencephalopathy) was linked to levamisole as a medicine, but the earlier review reports that no case acquired through cocaine had been reported, although its summary lists it among the consequences. Neither review gives how often these conditions occur among people exposed to levamisole through cocaine or weighs cocaine itself as a cause; the earlier review's statement that a significant minority of exposed people will be affected has no number behind it, and the later review's statement that the incidence is rising has no data behind it.
claims.magnitude: Second-hand. Levamisole in 73.2% of cocaine analysed by the US DEA in January 2010 (unsourced); in about 70% of US cocaine (2015 review); 1.5% to 4.1% of the sample in Luxembourg seizures; in 78% (Denver) and 88% (San Francisco) of urine samples screening positive for cocaine metabolites (2011). How often harm occurs among exposed people: not given by either source. Recovery in case reports: neutrophils within 2 to 3 days with GCSF in most reports, 5 to 10 days after exposure ended without it; skin lesions usually within a few weeks of stopping cocaine. Neutropenia in about half of vasculopathy cases; repeat agranulocytosis in about half of one series with renewed cocaine use.
